data.description:
# Game Design Document for AI_Hell

## Problem statement

The AI_Hell repository is a fresh start with no game content: it consists only of a README (which plans for a `docs/Game Design Document.md` and frames the project as an AI-framework tutorial) and workflow tooling. There is no design document, so neither human developers nor AI agents have an authoritative specification describing the game to build. This work item produces that document: a fully detailed Game Design Document (GDD) for **AI_Hell**, a 2D bullet hell game loosely based on Galaxians.

## Users

- **Human developers** following the README tutorial — need enough specification to implement the game without guesswork, while leaving space for AI/creative input.
- **AI agents** (coding assistants, Context Hub agents) — need a machine-readable, unambiguous specification with precise mechanics (movement, collision, bullets, waves, power-ups, scoring) so they can plan and implement against it.
- **Technical target audience** — the game is an AI-framework demonstration project, written for a technical audience; the GDD is a reference/tutorial artifact, not a commercial pitch.

### Example user stories

- As a **developer/AI agent**, I want the core gameplay loop defined precisely (enemy formations as the bullets, player movement, firing, power-up activation, enemy-fired projectiles in the pre-boss wave) so I can implement a coherent vertical slice.
- As a **developer/AI agent**, I want an explicit MVP scope (5 levels, 1 boss, 3 lives, ≥6 power-ups, local leaderboard, no difficulty scaling) so I can plan and estimate work.
- As a **developer**, I want a code-first technical architecture section that compares 2–3 code-first game engine options (no UI-heavy engine such as Godot/Unity) targeting web + Windows binary, so I can choose and set up the stack.
- As a **reader**, I want a Tron-inspired neon vector aesthetic defined so all art/UI decisions are consistent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1 — GDD artifact exists and covers game identity:** The document is created at `docs/Game Design Document.md` and opens with game identity: working title AI_Hell, genre (2D top-down bullet hell, Galaxians-inspired), a one-sentence pitch, target audience, and the Tron-inspired neon vector aesthetic direction.
- [ ] **AC2 — Core gameplay loop fully specified:** The document precisely specifies: formation waves whose enemies are themselves the collision threat ("the enemies are the bullets") in the first levels, with enemy-fired projectiles added in later levels; full 2D player movement (WASD/arrow keys); auto-fire; and Space as the activator for a movement-style power-up (e.g., dash/teleport). The GDD must be explicit that the **final wave of the MVP — the wave immediately before the boss — is an enemy-fired-projectile level**: it contains a smaller number of enemies than the earlier levels, but those enemies fire bullets in a predictable pattern.
- [ ] **AC3 — MVP vertical-slice content specified:** The GDD specifies a complete MVP vertical slice: **5 levels**, 1 boss encounter, 3 lives, at least 6 distinct power-up types, and a simple local leaderboard (local storage); difficulty scaling is explicitly out of scope for the MVP.
- [ ] **AC4 — Content catalog present:** The document includes catalogs with enough detail to implement: enemy types with formation/dive behaviors and bullet-pattern behavior (enemies-as-bullets vs. enemy-fired bullets, including the predictable pre-boss firing pattern), wave structure per level, the boss design, power-up list with effects, scoring system, and level progression.
- [ ] **AC5 — Technical architecture section:** The document specifies a code-first architecture that must run on the web and be distributable as a Windows binary, including: an engine policy (no engine with an extensive UI/editor such as Godot or Unity; code-first game engine libraries such as Phaser are allowed and encouraged), **2–3 concrete engine options with pros and cons for each**, a recommended stack, proposed module/file breakdown, entity/bullet/wave data model, save-data design (local storage), and key technical risks. The precise engine selection is left to the implementors.
- [ ] **AC6 — Validation:** The GDD is reviewed and accepted by the operator (producer review) against the interview answers captured in the clarifying-questions appendix; each major design decision is traceable to an answered question or a documented assumption.
- [ ] **AC7 — Documentation updated:** All related documentation is updated to reflect the changes, including code comments, README, and any relevant wiki or docs site entries (at minimum, README references to the GDD must match the new file).
- [ ] **AC8 — Test suite:** Full project test suite must pass with the new changes (a documentation-only change; run any existing checks/lint as applicable).

## Constraints

- The game must **run on the web** and be **distributable as a binary on Windows**.
- **Engine policy:** no engine with an extensive UI/editor (e.g., Godot or Unity). A **"code-first" game engine library (e.g., Phaser) is explicitly allowed and encouraged**. The precise engine selection is an implementor decision; the GDD must present 2–3 engine options with pros and cons for each.
- This is a **tutorial/demonstration project** for AI-assisted development (Context Hub), not a fully releasable commercial game; scope is a vertical slice.
- Working title is **AI_Hell**; genre is **2D bullet hell, loosely based on Galaxians**.
- MVP scope is fixed: **5 levels**, 1 boss, 3 lives, ≥6 power-ups, local leaderboard; **no difficulty scaling in the MVP**.
- Aesthetic: **neon vector, Tron-inspired**.

## Existing state

- Repository contains only `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `.gitignore`, `.githooks/`, and `.worklog/` — no game code or design content.
- `README.md` already plans for a `docs/Game Design Document.md` and documents the work-item workflow (Idea → Intake → Plan → In Review → Release). It frames the game as "a classic Bullet Hell game written to demonstrate the use of the Context Hub AI framework... written by humans for a technical target audience."
- No existing work items related to the game design (this item is the first).

## Desired change

A comprehensive GDD at `docs/Game Design Document.md` that enables both humans and AI agents to **guide the development of the game in a consistent way** - an authoritative design reference for all subsequent game development work items. The document is a **living document**: it may be edited during development as the game evolves, and such changes are expected to be tracked in the worklog so decisions remain traceable.

## Key Files

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — **the deliverable**; new comprehensive design document (identity, core loop, MVP scope, content catalogs, technical architecture with engine options, risks).
- `README.md` — verify/update references so the tutorial points to the correct GDD path (minor).

## Technical architecture recommendation (proposed assumption, to be confirmed at planning)

Engine policy: **code-first only** — no engine with an extensive UI/editor (e.g., Godot, Unity). Code-first game engine libraries are allowed and encouraged; final selection is the implementors' decision. The GDD must present the following options with pros and cons:

1. **Phaser (TypeScript/HTML5)** — pro: mature 2D game framework with scenes, physics, tweens, and input out of the box; large ecosystem and docs; fast to scaffold, ideal for a tutorial. Con: opinionated framework layer over the raw game loop; some abstraction to learn.
2. **PixiJS + hand-written game loop (TypeScript)** — pro: rendering-focused WebGL library, maximum code control, excellent for teaching the game loop/entity systems by hand. Con: no built-in scene/physics/collision — more boilerplate.
3. **Plain HTML5 Canvas + TypeScript (no game library)** — pro: zero dependencies, maximum didactic value for an AI-framework tutorial. Con: input, loop, collision, and rendering all hand-rolled; slowest to build.

Distribution: package the same web codebase as a **Windows binary with Tauri v2** (lightweight, code-first) or Electron (heavier). **Persistence:** `localStorage` for the MVP leaderboard and save data.

## Related work

- `README.md` (repository root) — project framing and tutorial context; planned GDD path.
- No related worklog work items; this item is the seed for all subsequent game work.

## Risks and assumptions

- **Scope creep risk:** the GDD must stay a vertical-slice specification; extra opportunities (difficulty scaling, online leaderboards, more levels, online multiplayer) should be recorded as linked future work items, not added to the MVP.
- **Engine selection:** the concrete engine (Phaser vs. PixiJS vs. plain Canvas, among code-first options) is an implementation decision; the GDD must document 2–3 options with pros/cons, and selection may vary during planning as long as the code-first/web + Windows binary constraints hold.
- **"Enemies are the bullets" ambiguity risk:** the document must crisply define the collision/lethality model (player dies on contact with enemies in early waves; bullets become a secondary threat later, notably in the predictable-pattern pre-boss wave) so implementations do not diverge.
- **AI creativity pacing:** per README guidance, the GDD should nail the core loop in detail while leaving reasonable space for AI suggestions in non-core areas (e.g., art details, pattern variations).

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers

- Q1: "Gameplay structure — how 'loosely' based on Galaxians? ... player movement — horizontal-only lanes, or free 2D movement?" — Answer (user): "Lets have enemies in formation waves that are themselves the bullets. In later waves the enemies may also fire bullets, but in the first levels they are the bullets. The player has full 2d movement." Source: interactive reply (round 1). **Revised (final accepted answer):** see Q7 — the enemy-fired-bullets capability is made explicit as the final pre-boss wave of the MVP.
- Q2: "Theme & fiction — what does 'AI_Hell' mean narratively? ... And what visual aesthetic ...?" — Answer (user): "I really like your proposal. Lets go with that. In terms of visual aesthetic I think we need to go with a neon vector approach inspired by Tron." Accepted fiction: hellscape ruled by rogue/berserk AI constructs; player pilots a ship through an AI-generated underworld; enemies are literal AI manifestations. Source: interactive reply (round 1).
- Q3: "Scope & structure for a tutorial/demo game ... how many stages for the MVP vision?" — Answer (user): "The MVP should be a vertical slice of the proposed game. Lets say 3 levels, a single boss, 3 lives, at least 6 kinds of power up, leaderboard. We don't need difficulty scaling in the MVP." Source: interactive reply (round 1). **Revised (final accepted answer):** 5 levels — see Q8.
- Q4: "Technology target — should the GDD target a specific stack ... or stay engine-agnostic?" — Answer (user): "You can choose the technical stack. The requirements are that it must run on the web and be distributable as a binary on Windows. We should not use Godot or another such engine, lets focus on a code-first approach." Source: interactive reply (round 2). **Revised (final accepted answer):** see Q9 — "no engine" clarified to mean no UI-heavy engine (Godot/Unity); code-first engines (e.g., Phaser) are explicitly allowed.
- Q5: "Controls & input — keyboard/mouse/gamepad?" — Answer (user): "WASD/Arrow keys, auto-fire, space as an activator for a movement powerup (e.g. dash, teleport from danger)." Source: interactive reply (round 2).
- Q6: "Leaderboard persistence — simple local leaderboard, or online via a backend?" — Answer (user): "simple local storage is sufficient for the MVP." Source: interactive reply (round 2).
- Q7: "AC2 — can we be explicit about enemy-fired projectiles? Should the final wave of the MVP (before the boss) be such a level?" — Answer (user): "Yes — the final wave of the MVP (before the boss) will have such a level. There will be a smaller number of enemies in this level, but they will fire bullets in a predictable pattern." Source: interactive reply (revision round). Prior answer (Q1) left the enemy-firing capability as "later waves may fire bullets"; final accepted answer makes the pre-boss wave an explicit enemy-fired-projectile level with fewer enemies and predictable firing patterns.
- Q8: "AC3 — how many levels should the MVP have?" — Answer (user): "Increase the number of levels to 5." Source: interactive reply (revision round). Prior answer (Q3): 3 levels; final accepted answer: 5 levels.
- Q9: "'No engine' / 'code-first' could be misread as banning game engine libraries — clarify engine policy?" — Answer (user): "We don't want to use an Engine with an extensive UI (e.g. Godot or Unity), but we do want to leverage a 'code-first' engine (e.g. Phaser). The precise engine selected is up to the implementors. Present 2-3 options listing the pros and cons of each." Source: interactive reply (revision round).

- Q10: "Desired change says the GDD will let agents build 'without further clarification' - is that too restrictive?" - Answer (user): "Yes - too restrictive and unrealistic. The goal is a document that will enable agents and humans to guide development of the game in a consistent way. The document itself should be considered a living document and may be edited during development." Source: interactive reply (revision round). Prior text: 'without further clarification'; final accepted answer: consistent-guidance goal + living-document status.

# Write the Game Design Document for AI_Hell

## Goal

Create a comprehensive Game Design Document (GDD) at `docs/Game Design Document.md` that serves as the authoritative design reference for both human developers and AI agents building the AI_Hell game.

## Scope

The GDD must cover:

1. **Game Identity**: Working title, genre (2D top-down bullet hell, Galaxians-inspired), one-sentence pitch, target audience, Tron-inspired neon vector aesthetic.
2. **Core Gameplay Loop**: Formation waves (enemies-as-bullets in early levels), enemy-fired projectiles in later levels, full 2D player movement (WASD/arrow keys), auto-fire, Space as movement power-up activator. Explicitly: the final wave before the boss is an enemy-fired-projectile level with fewer enemies and predictable firing patterns.
3. **MVP Vertical-Slice Content**: 5 levels, 1 boss encounter, 3 lives, 6+ distinct power-up types, simple local leaderboard (localStorage); difficulty scaling explicitly out of scope.
4. **Content Catalogs**:
   - Enemy types with formation/dive behaviors, bullet-pattern behavior (enemies-as-bullets vs enemy-fired bullets)
   - Wave structure per level
   - Boss design
   - Power-up list with effects
   - Scoring system
   - Level progression
5. **Technical Architecture**: Code-first engine policy (no UI-heavy engines like Godot/Unity), 2-3 concrete engine options with pros/cons (e.g., Phaser, PixiJS+hand-written loop, Plain HTML5 Canvas), recommended stack, module/file breakdown, entity/bullet/wave data model, save-data design (localStorage), key technical risks.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] **AC1**: Document exists at `docs/Game Design Document.md`
- [ ] **AC2**: Game identity section present (title, genre, pitch, audience, aesthetic)
- [ ] **AC3**: Core gameplay loop fully specified (formation waves, 2D movement, auto-fire, power-up, enemy-fired projectiles in pre-boss wave)
- [ ] **AC4**: MVP content specified (5 levels, 1 boss, 3 lives, 6+ power-ups, local leaderboard, no difficulty scaling)
- [ ] **AC5**: Content catalogs present (enemies, waves, boss, power-ups, scoring, progression)
- [ ] **AC6**: Technical architecture section with 2-3 engine options, pros/cons, module breakdown, data model, save design, risks

## Constraints

- Working title: **AI_Hell**
- Genre: **2D bullet hell, loosely based on Galaxians**
- Engine policy: **code-first only** (no Godot/Unity); code-first engines (Phaser, PixiJS, plain Canvas) allowed
- Must run on web, distributable as Windows binary
- Tutorial/demonstration project for AI-assisted development
- Aesthetic: **neon vector, Tron-inspired**
- The GDD is a **living document** — may be edited during development with worklog-tracked changes

## Appendix: clarifying questions & answers (from parent AH-0MT7O8KCY0059RA5)

- Q1: Gameplay structure — enemies in formation waves as bullets, full 2D movement. Final accepted: enemy-fired projectiles in pre-boss wave.
- Q2: Theme — hellscape ruled by rogue AI; Tron-inspired neon vector aesthetic.
- Q3: Scope — revised from 3 to 5 levels.
- Q4: Tech stack — web + Windows binary, code-first (no UI-heavy engines).
- Q5: Controls — WASD/Arrows, auto-fire, Space for power-up.
- Q6: Leaderboard — simple localStorage for MVP.
- Q7: Pre-boss wave explicitly enemy-fired-projectile with fewer enemies, predictable patterns.
- Q8: MVP expanded from 3 to 5 levels.
- Q9: Engine policy clarified — code-first engines (Phaser etc.) explicitly allowed.
- Q10: GDD is a living document enabling consistent guidance, not a rigid spec.

## Key Files

- `docs/Game Design Document.md` — **the deliverable**; new comprehensive design document.
